title: VB9-10192
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): She is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated November 29, 2019, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Vietnam. She is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated November 29, 2019, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.

I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The determinative issues in this appeal are credibility and the availability of an internal flight alternative (IFA).

The Appellant alleges a fear of her husband, whom she married in 2008, and who is a womanizing, gambling, drug addicted criminal. He is 10 years older than the Appellant and was married twice before. The Appellant alleges that her husband beat her frequently during their marriage. She is reluctant to file for divorce for fear of being beaten, and did not approach the police for help as she believes that they would treat it as a private family matter. The Appellant alleges to have escaped from her husband on three occasions, in 2011, 2013, and in 2016. On the first two occasions she was captured by his underlings and returned to him. In 2016, the Appellant alleges she was caught by her husband at the airport when she was trying to flee to Ho Chi Minh City. However, she deceived him by asking him to allow her to go have her hair done for a wedding they were to attend that same day. She took that opportunity to go back to the airport and flee to Ho Chi Minh City, where she remained in hiding until she received her Canadian visa. She flew to Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, residing with her permanent resident sister in British Colombia and made a claim for refugee protection on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, after her application for a work permit was denied. The Appellant alleges that her husband continues to harass her parents.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1

The RPD accepted that the Appellant was in an abusive domestic relationship, but also determined that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Ho Chi Minh City and that it would not be unreasonable for her to relocate there. The Appellant argues that this was an erroneous finding, that Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City are not as large as they sound, and that the Appellant's husband would be motivated to find her because she is young and could care for him. After conducting an independent analysis, I too find that there is a viable IFA for the Appellant in Ho Chi Minh City.

The Federal Court of Appeal (FCA), in Rasaratnam,2 provides that the test to be applied in determining whether there is an IFA is two-pronged: (1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists. (2) And the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.

The FCA went on to provide guidance with respect to the "unreasonableness test" in the second prong of the test in Thirunavukkarasu.3 It spelled out a very high threshold regarding what makes an IFA unreasonable in all of the circumstances. Hardship that is associated with dislocation and relocation is not one that would render an IFA unreasonable. The Appellant is required to provide proof of adverse conditions which would jeopardize her life and safety in travelling to and in living in the IFA location.

For the Appellant to have an IFA, both prongs of the test must be satisfied. The onus shifts to the Appellant to prove that she does not have an IFA once the issue has been raised and potential IFAs have been proposed. Is there a serious possibility of persecution in Ho Chi Minh City?

According to the World Fact Book,4 Vietnam is the world's 15th most populous nation with a population approaching 100 million as of July 2017. The country has a land mass of over 330,000 square kilometres. The capital city of Hanoi has a population approaching eight million, and Ho Chi Minh City has a population of almost nine million.

The RPD accepted that the Appellant was in an abusive domestic relationship. For the purposes of this appeal, I accept without deciding, that the Appellant was in such a relationship. The RPD also determined that there was insufficient evidence that the Appellant's husband has the ability or access to information that would result in him being able to locate the Appellant throughout Vietnam. Further, the RPD determined that the husband was not motivated to continue to locate her if she lived elsewhere in Vietnam. The Appellant argues that her husband would be able to find her through his extensive network and that her age distinguishes her from his previous wives in terms of his motivation to pursue her.

Once an IFA is identified, the onus shifts to the Appellant to establish that a serious possibility of persecution or risk of danger exists if she were to locate there. I find that the Appellant's husband would not locate her if she were to travel to Ho Chi Minh City.

A review of the record shows that the Appellant described her husband as a leader of a gang in her home city of Haiphong, who extorted money from local businesses.5 Despite being married to him since 2008 she did not know of anything else that he did. The record reveals no evidence of the husband having any connections or business outside of Haiphong, and no evidence whatsoever that he had an extensive network as the Appellant argues. The Appellant testified that she first escaped her husband in 2011 when she went to Hanoi, but after three weeks, while she went out to look for a job, her husband's staff members simply found her because they all knew her.6 The Appellant testified that she did not know how they found her in Hanoi. I do not find it credible, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's husband's staff, for whom there is no evidence of having any connections outside of Haiphong, would randomly locate her in front of her apartment, in a city of almost eight million people, in a country that is over 300,000 square kilometres large, and has a population approaching 100 million.

The Appellant also argues that the reason her husband's underlings found her in Hanoi is because people of Haiphong are often tightly connected and in touch with each other wherever they might be currently living. This is mere speculation; the Appellant has not provided any evidence to support this cultural practice. Her testimony is that she had a friend in Hanoi that she met in Hong Kong and kept in touch with.7 There is no other evidence that she was in touch with any persons from Haiphong as the Appellant asserts. Further, there is no evidence to support the Appellant's argument that her husband somehow followed her parents to Hanoi when they were bringing her supplies. There is no mention in her narrative or in her testimony of her parents bringing her supplies in Hanoi. The Appellant has not credibly established that she was located by her husband or that she fled to Hanoi in 2011.

In 2013, the Appellant alleged that she once again fled her husband. She testified that she flew to Ho Chi Minh City, a city some 1800 kilometres away, where she remained for two weeks until a neighbour called her to tell her that her husband was flying there, so she flew to Hanoi a second time, and remained there for two more weeks until she was again found.8 A review of the Appellant's testimony shows that the neighbour did not know that the Appellant was in Ho Chi Minh City but called her anyways to tell her that her husband was flying to Ho Chi Minh City to look for her.9 Further, the Appellant testified that she had changed her phone SIM card after she arrived in Ho Chi Minh City and her phone number was different from that in Haiphong.10 The evidence suggests that the neighbour did not have the new phone number of the Appellant. I do not find it credible that a neighbour would call the Appellant on a phone number she did not have, in a city she did not know the Appellant was in, to tell her that her husband was flying to that very same city to look for her. Further, in her narrative the Appellant states that she was found in Hanoi by her husband and his underlings and dragged back to Haiphong.11 In her testimony the Appellant stated that her husband alone came to her place to find her.12 This inconsistency in her evidence impugns the Appellant's allegation that she escaped and was located in 2013.

In 2016, the Appellant alleges to have fled once again. In her narrative she writes that she was at the airport trying to flee when her husband caught her.13 She was able, ultimately, to flee back to the airport and onwards to Ho Chi Minh City again, simply by asking her husband to let her go have her hair done for a wedding they were to attend that night. I do not find this to be a reasonable explanation. The Appellant testified that the nature of her relationship with her husband was such that she was not allowed to do anything, to go out, or have a relationship with anyone.14 Yet, after having attempted to flee him on two previous occasions, and after just being caught by her husband attempting a third escape to the airport, it is not credible, on a balance, that he would just allow her to go get her hair done, and thus be able to flee to Ho Chi Minh City.

Further, despite living in Hanoi in a rented apartment for three weeks in 2011, living in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi for one month in 2013, and living in Ho Chi Minh City again in 2016, and after stating in her Basis of Claim (BOC) form that she had moved to another part of Vietnam to seek safety, the Appellant never listed these addresses in her forms. When this omission was put to the Appellant, she testified that she had declared to her counsel that she went to Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. This is not a credible reply. The BOC is clear regarding the requirement to list all of the addresses that she lived in over the last 10 years, and the Appellant declared the information in her BOC to be complete, true, and correct. The Appellant has not credibly established that she escaped to Ho Chi Minh City in 2016.

Also, the Appellant testified that her husband continues to harass her parents in Vietnam regarding her return, so much so that she and her sister had to have cameras installed at their parents' home.15 He frequently visits her parents and threatens them.16 This is inconsistent with a letter from the Appellant's parents17 who outline one instance of her husband visiting them and that this had angered them. When this inconsistency was put to the Appellant by the RPD she only confirmed that they cited just the one incident. I prefer the evidence of the parents, who are describing in their own words their interaction with and feelings about their son-in-law.

Her parents live on the other side of the riverbank from her husband18, yet in the three years since she left Vietnam her husband has only gone to her parents' home once to look for her. Further, the RPD determined that the Appellant's allegation of her parents being threatened was eroded by the absence of any efforts to move her parents away from her husband. The Appellant argues that this was a mischaracterization, that the Appellant's sister simply did not have the finances to sponsor her parents to come to Canada. On the contrary, the Appellant testified that her parents were old and did not want to come to Canada.19 There is no mention in the evidence of finances being an issue. Also, the evidence does not support the Appellant's assertion that her parents could not move within Vietnam because in so doing they would have to reveal their new address to the local police, and by extension to her husband given his connection to the police. There is no mention in the record of her husband having any connection to the police. I find that, on a balance, the evidence does not demonstrate that the Appellant's parents continue to be harassed by her husband, and this undermines the Appellant's allegations that her husband is motivated to find her via her parents.

The Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that her husband has the motivation and means to locate her in Ho Chi Minh City. I find that the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution in Ho Chi Minh City. Is it unreasonable, in all the circumstances, for the Appellant to relocate to Ho Chi Minh City?

As mentioned above, the threshold for unreasonableness is set very high. The RPD, after reviewing the objective documentary evidence, determined it is reasonable for the Appellant to seek refuge in Ho Chi Minh City. The Appellant has not contested this finding. I find that the RPD determination was correct and the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that she would face undue hardship in relocation to Ho Chi Minh City.

The RPD, in its decision, states that it took into account the contents of the Chairperson's Guideline 4 - Women refugee claimants fearing gender related persecution.20 In doing so, the RPD considered various social, economic, and cultural factors. Similarly, the RPD states that it considered the country condition evidence which is contained in the National Documentation Package (NDP). An independent analysis of the objective country evidence shows that women in Vietnam can do most things on their own with very few restrictions, and there are no restrictions on single or divorced women living alone.21 The same evidence indicates that although women who live alone are generally poorly perceived, these cultural tendencies are changing and that in larger cities where neighbours do not know one another that is not the situation. The evidence suggests that women and men can relocate freely in Vietnam, but it is easier for women to relocate in large cities like Hanoi, and that educated women have an advantage at finding work and accommodations. The Appellant is an educated woman, having completed high school in Vietnam.22 She has significant experience as a nail technician both in Canada and in Vietnam,23 and continues to have the support of her sister and her parents. I find that the Appellant will be able to support herself in Ho Chi Minh City.

The Appellant has the ability to travel to the IFA in Ho Chi Minh City. It is serviced by an international airport, and she could travel there directly. The Appellant has travelled to Ho Chi Minh City on at least three occasions and remained there in 2016, living with a friend while awaiting her visa. I also note that the Appellant has also previously relocated to Hong Kong and Canada. As a result, I find that she could reasonably relocate to Ho Chi Minh City. The record also shows that the Appellant did not identify any factors, other than those relating to the fear of her husband, that would limit her ability to relocate to or cause her any undue hardship in relocating to Ho Chi Minh City.24

Based upon all the evidence, I find that a viable IFA does exist for the Appellant. I find that there is not a serious possibility that the Appellant would be persecuted if she returned to Vietnam, pursuant to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). I also find, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant would not be personally subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Vietnam, pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) Ron Stratigopoulos R.
